sections.h2: Broken Arrow housing at a glance
sections.html:
Broken Arrow covers about 45 square miles in the northeast corner of Oklahoma, in the region called Green Country. The 2020 census counted 113,540 residents, making it the fourth most populous city in the state, and the Tulsa metro area had 1,023,988. Most of the city lies in Tulsa County, with some areas extending into Wagoner County and zoned to Broken Arrow Public Schools.

A house near the downtown Main Street area, one by the Creek Turnpike on the south side and one on the Wagoner County edge sit in different pockets with different commutes and different county offices. Green Country has hills and lakes, so lots can slope or sit near creeks more than the flat plains image suggests.

The city stayed small until the 1960s, when the Broken Arrow Expressway, State Highway 51, linked it to downtown Tulsa. Population went from a little above 11,000 in 1970 to more than 50,000 in 1990 and over 74,000 by 2000, so much of the housing dates from the 1970s onward. Retail buyers often ask for repairs on houses that need updating.

Three districts serve Broken Arrow addresses: Broken Arrow Public Schools, Union Public Schools and Bixby Public Schools. In Tulsa County, most of the city is in Broken Arrow Public Schools, the northwestern area is in Union, and a far southwest area is in Bixby. Two similar houses a few blocks apart can feed different schools, and buyers check this early, so know your district.

State Highway 51 crosses the north side of the city and leads northwest to downtown Tulsa. Heading east, it connects to the Muskogee Turnpike. The Creek Turnpike curves around the south side and links the Turner Turnpike with the Will Rogers Turnpike. Tulsa Transit runs one route between Broken Arrow and Tulsa on weekdays, so most households rely on cars. Being near an expressway entrance helps a sale, and being beside a busy road hurts it.

The city's Inspections division checks that new structures and modifications meet adopted codes, inspects each phase of construction, issues certificates of occupancy and investigates alleged violations. It also addresses unsafe or unsanitary buildings that endanger occupants or the neighborhood.

The city has adopted the 2024 international residential, building, fire, mechanical and fuel gas codes and the 2023 National Electric Code, each as amended by the state and the city. Schedule inspections through the city's online self-service portal.

If you finished a garage, added a bedroom or replaced a furnace, find the permit and sign-off. Open or missing records can slow a conventional buyer's financing, while a direct buyer will usually talk about the house as it stands.

One monthly statement from the city covers water, sanitary sewer, curbside trash, stormwater, streetlight and LifeRide. You manage the account through the Water Smart portal. Gas comes from Oklahoma Natural Gas and electric from Public Service Company of Oklahoma.

Utility chargeAmount or rule
Deposit, new residential customer$100, refundable, may be waived after a favorable credit check
Start or transfer fee$30, non-refundable
Bill due dateNo earlier than 20 days after the billing date
Late fee10 percent after 5:00 p.m. the day after the due date

When you sell, schedule a stop or transfer in Water Smart so your final bill closes on the sale date. Unpaid city charges can become a closing headache. Utility Billing is at 116 E Dallas Street.

The Tulsa County Assessor values each Broken Arrow property as of January 1 and revalues residential property every year. A valuation notice gives you 30 calendar days to protest in writing, and an informal protest can happen by phone.

Assessed value is 11 percent of taxable fair cash value. Taxable value is capped at a 5 percent yearly rise, or 3 percent with a homestead, but the cap is removed when the property is purchased. A new owner therefore sees a bigger bill than the previous one, and the assessor lists that among its common questions.

Homestead applications are due by March 15 or within 30 days of the increase notice to count for the current year. You owe the whole year's bill on a property as it stood on January 1, even if you sell part of it later.

Tax that is still owing when the house sells is usually deducted from your proceeds at closing. Get the balance from the county treasurer before listing, and find out whether your lot sits in Tulsa County or the Wagoner County portion.

  1. Work out which county handles your parcel.
  2. Ask the treasurer to write down what you owe.
  3. Look for permits and final inspections on any garage, bedroom or furnace project.
  4. Use Water Smart to stop or move your utilities as of the sale date.

Dated houses are a tougher sell on the open market because a lender often insists on repairs first. A direct buyer is usually fine without them.

sections.h2: How a quick sale works here
sections.html:
Buyers will want a handful of answers: the county and school district, permits for any finished work, and the age of the roof, furnace and air conditioning. With those in hand, weigh two paths. An agent listing may fetch more for a house that shows well, though you take on showings, inspection requests and a wait for financing. A direct cash purchase usually drops those steps and settles on a date you pick.

Broken Arrow grew as a bedroom community for Tulsa workers, and it also has the third-largest concentration of manufacturers in Oklahoma, so buyers arrive from several directions. Houses near the expressway or a turnpike entrance tend to draw commuters, while a Wagoner County address may raise questions about which offices you deal with.

Heat and cold are hard on equipment here, so expect questions about the age of the cooling system. Either way, assemble the same documents: tax notice, deed, permit sign-offs and a final utility date. A complete folder keeps closing day on schedule.

Deeds carry a documentary stamp tax of 75 cents on each $500 of consideration, set by 68 O.S. section 3201 and affixed by the clerk at filing.

Oklahoma sellers of one- and two-family homes must give the buyer a written condition disclosure or a disclaimer statement under 60 O.S. section 833. Exempt transfers, such as gifts without consideration, need the exemption noted on the deed.

Heat and cold are tough on a house here. Summers average a high near 92.9 F in July, and January lows near 22.2 F test pipes and cooling systems alike, so a buyer's inspector will test both. Annual precipitation runs about 38.9 inches.

faqs.q: Is Broken Arrow in Tulsa County?
faqs.a: Mostly. The city is in Tulsa County, with a portion that extends into Wagoner County. Your tax notice shows which county assessor and clerk handle the property.

faqs.q: Which school district is my Broken Arrow house in?
faqs.a: It depends on the address. Most Tulsa County addresses are in Broken Arrow Public Schools, the northwest corner is in Union and a far southwest area is in Bixby.

faqs.q: What deposit does Broken Arrow charge for new utility service?
faqs.a: A refundable $100 deposit for new residential customers, plus a $30 non-refundable start or transfer fee. Call Utility Billing at 116 E Dallas Street for specifics.

faqs.q: Does the Tulsa County cap on taxable value apply after I sell?
faqs.a: No. The cap is removed when a property is purchased, so the buyer's taxable value can reset to current market value.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Broken Arrow house without making repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Many direct buyers purchase as-is. You still owe the written disclosure or disclaimer statement under Oklahoma law.
